slides.title: What does USDJPY rising actually mean?
lines: “Dollar/yen went up — does that mean the yen is stronger?”
No. More yen per US dollar means yen weakened against USD.

slides.title: Why JXY can contradict your USDJPY chart
lines: USDJPY reacts to both US and Japanese factors.
A yen index responds to JPY against several currencies.
TVC symbols are calculated by TradingView; source can differ from exchange pricing.
Document the exact symbol, feed and index formula before using JXY as a test.

slides.title: Higher US yields may support USDJPY — but not always
lines: Rising expected US-Japan rate spread can support USDJPY when other drivers are held fixed.
Risk-off, repatriation, hedging cost and leverage unwinds can dominate yield spreads.
An observed USDJPY drop alone does not prove a yen-funded carry liquidation.

slides.title: An oil shock has several possible pathways
lines: Oil exporters and importers face different terms-of-trade effects; no fixed USDJPY rule.

slides.title: Why an inverse USD–oil chart is not a law
lines: A stronger dollar can raise local-currency commodity costs for some importing buyers.
War, refinery bottlenecks or shipping disruption can overwhelm the FX channel.
Check benchmark contract/tenor, product cracks and actual oil inventories.

slides.title: What four different shocks could look like
lines: Yields and USD may rise; oil demand and cyclicals conditional.
JPY and USD may both gain versus risk currencies; equities suffer.
Oil/product prices rise; inflation and growth channels compete.
JPY funding repaid; leveraged equities may be sold.
These are hypothesis templates, not correlations that always hold.
